glossary.def: A crystalline material only one or a few atoms thick, such as graphene. Its thinness gives it electronic, optical and mechanical properties unlike the bulk form.
A chemically modified RNA building block with an extra methyl group. Found in RNA caps and some transfer RNAs, where it helps stability and protein production.
Adeno-associated virus: a small, mild virus that is stripped of its own genes and used as a vehicle to deliver therapeutic genes into cells.
The rule that a material that absorbs light strongly also emits it strongly. In solar cells it means good absorbers tend to lose energy quickly by emitting light.
A small, simple marine worm without a gut cavity. Some species host algae in their bodies and are used to study regeneration and symbiosis.
The part of the daily cycle when an animal is awake and active, which in mice is the night.
The mixing of genetic ancestry when previously separate populations interbreed.
A genus of gut bacteria that feeds on the gut's mucus layer. Akkermansia muciniphila is linked to metabolism and responses to immunotherapy.
The ability of an organism to tell its own cells or tissues from those of genetically different members of the same species.
A type of magnet whose atomic magnetic moments cancel out overall, like an antiferromagnet, yet whose electrons still behave as if spin-split, as in a ferromagnet.
An almond-shaped group of nerve cells deep in each side of the brain that helps process emotions, especially fear and threat.
A type of protein clump in which many copies of a protein stack into long, stable fibres. Often linked to disease, but some amyloids do normal jobs in cells.
Genetic material recovered from old remains such as bones and teeth, used to study past populations and their movements.
Reduction of the body's detection of or response to painful stimuli, as measured in animal studies.
A small flowering plant in the mustard family (thale cress), used as the standard model organism in plant biology because of its small genome and short life cycle.
A single-celled microbe without a nucleus that forms a separate domain of life from bacteria. Some groups are the closest known relatives of complex cells.
A transcription factor that drives neuroendocrine identity in nerve-like cells and defines a major subtype of small cell lung cancer.
A lab-grown 3D tissue model that combines different cell types or mini-organs, such as tumour cells with their supporting cells.
A sequencing method that finds which parts of the genome are open and accessible, which marks DNA regions likely to control gene activity.
A reaction where a catalyst moves a halogen atom so that a radical joins across a carbon-carbon double bond, making a single new product.
A controlled way to make plastics in which a metal catalyst switches growing polymer chains on and off by moving a halogen atom.
A billionth of a billionth of a second. Laser pulses this short can capture the motion of electrons.
A family of protein machines, also called SWI/SNF, that move or loosen packaged DNA to control gene access. Its genes are often mutated in cancer.
A property of a material's electron energy bands, described by whole-number invariants, that stays the same under smooth changes and leads to protected edge or surface states.
The energy gap an electron must jump to conduct electricity in a solid. Metals have no gap, semiconductors a small one, insulators a large one.
Tetrahydrobiopterin: a helper molecule needed by several enzymes that make neurotransmitters and nitric oxide. It also acts as an antioxidant in cell membranes.
A molecule made from cholesterol in the liver that helps digest fats. Gut bacteria modify bile acids into forms with different signalling effects.
A compound of bismuth and sulfur that behaves as a semiconductor. It absorbs visible light well and is studied for solar cells and light detectors.
A tight lining of blood vessels in the brain that controls which substances pass from blood into brain tissue.
The internal timekeeper that runs on a roughly 24-hour cycle and times sleep, hormone release and other daily rhythms; it is reset mainly by light.
A wave state that stays trapped and does not leak away even though its energy lies within a range of freely moving states. Known in optics and now sought in electronics.
The basic range of electron momentum values in a crystal. Plotting electron energies across it shows a material's electronic band structure.
An increase in the number of repeated CAG DNA units in a gene. In Huntington's disease, longer repeats cause disease, and repeats can keep lengthening in some cells over life.
A connective-tissue cell in a tumour that has been changed by cancer cells and helps shape tumour growth, immune responses and drug response.
A T cell engineered to carry a chimeric antigen receptor, which lets it recognise and kill cells with a chosen surface target, used against blood cancers.
A molecule containing a carbon atom with only two bonds and two unshared electrons, often reactive and sometimes magnetic.
One of 23 standard stages used to describe human embryo development over the first eight weeks, based on visible features rather than exact age.
A small molecule, rich in red meat, that carries fatty acids into mitochondria so they can be burned for energy.
A widespread black crow of Europe and Asia, Corvus corone. Crows are highly intelligent birds used in studies of cognition.
A network of nerve cells that produces rhythmic output, such as walking, breathing or swimming movements, without needing rhythmic input from the senses or brain.
A group of marine molluscs including squid, octopus and cuttlefish, known for large brains and complex behaviour.
A helper protein that assists other proteins in folding into the right shape, prevents them from clumping, and helps refold or clear damaged ones.
Cancer treatment with drugs that block brake molecules on T cells, such as PD-1 or CTLA-4, so the immune system attacks tumours more strongly.
A metallic state whose electron bands carry a nonzero topological whole-number invariant, so it shows a strong Hall effect and edge currents while its interior still conducts.
A conducting channel along the edge of a topological material in which electrons travel in only one direction, so they resist backscattering.
Handedness: the property of an object or motion that cannot be superimposed on its mirror image, like left and right hands. Applies to molecules, crystals and waves.
How open or loosely packed a stretch of DNA is. Open regions can be reached by proteins that switch genes on or off.
A method that uses antibodies to pull down a chosen protein with the DNA it is bound to, showing where that protein sits on the genome.
A folded stretch of DNA that brings two distant sites, such as a gene's start and a control region, into contact.
A DNA variant linked to how open a nearby stretch of chromatin is. Helps explain how variants outside genes affect gene control.
The difference in how a material absorbs left- and right-circularly polarised light. It reveals handedness in molecules or, in magnetic materials, the direction of magnetisation.
A cancer cell that has broken away from a tumour and travels in the blood. Such cells can seed metastases.
Small pieces of DNA released by tumours into the blood. Measured by blood test to track cancer, treatment response or remaining disease.
A spore-forming bacterium that makes many toxins and can cause food poisoning, gas gangrene and gut infections.
An emotion-control strategy of rethinking the meaning of a situation to change how one feels about it.
A ring-shaped protein complex that holds copied chromosomes together and extrudes DNA loops that organize the genome in 3D.
Describes microbes that live on or in a host normally without causing harm, such as the usual bacteria of the skin and gut.
A DNA difference carried by a sizeable share of the population, usually more than about one percent. Each one typically has only a small effect on disease risk.
Triggering of the complement system, a cascade of blood proteins that tags and destroys microbes and drives inflammation. Uncontrolled activation can damage the body's own tissues.
The basic unit of electrical conductance for one perfect channel in a nanoscale conductor, set by fundamental constants.
A complete wiring map of all nerve cells and their connections in a nervous system or part of it.
The splitting of a continent into separate pieces by stretching of its crust, which can lead to formation of a new ocean basin.
A stretch of DNA that is deleted or duplicated, so a cell has fewer or more copies of it than usual.
A large, structured collection of texts or recordings gathered for systematic analysis, as of a language or animal songs.
A gene-editing system adapted from bacterial immunity in which a guide RNA leads an enzyme such as Cas9 to a chosen DNA site to cut or change it.
An experiment that uses CRISPR gene editing to switch off many genes, one per cell, to find which genes matter for a chosen effect.
A DNA-binding protein that marks boundaries in the genome and helps fold DNA into loops, shaping which genes and control regions meet.
An inherited mitochondrial disorder in which the last enzyme complex of the electron transport chain (complex IV) works poorly, often affecting brain, muscle, heart and liver.
A molecule released from damaged or stressed cells, or from microbes, that warns the immune system and triggers inflammation.
A genus of tiny freshwater fish related to zebrafish that stay transparent and have a small brain as adults, making them useful for imaging the whole animal.
Searching large datasets with automated methods to find patterns, relationships or candidates that would be hard to spot by hand.
An antibody-drug conjugate that uses an antibody against the protein TROP2 to deliver a cell-killing drug directly to cancer cells.
A drug that removes a disease-related protein by steering the cell's own protein-destruction machinery onto it, instead of simply blocking the protein's activity.
The spreading of electrons over many atoms or a whole material rather than being tied to one atom or bond. It underlies metallic conduction and long-range electronic effects.
Breaking a polymer back down into its small building blocks, which can enable true recycling.
A biological cycle that follows the 24-hour day-night cycle, for example changes in activity or behaviour between day and night.
A single-celled, mostly marine alga, often with two whip-like tails. Some live inside animals such as corals and supply them with food made by photosynthesis.
The direct magnetic interaction between two magnetic moments through space, like the pull between two small bar magnets. It is weak but can split energy levels.
The movement of individuals away from where they were born to new places to live and breed. It links populations and spreads genes.
A collection of many genetically different lines or varieties of a species, studied together to link natural genetic differences to traits.
Adding or removing electrons in a material, by chemical substitution or an electric gate, to tune its properties. Removing electrons creates holes.
A side effect severe enough to prevent raising a drug's dose any further, used in early trials to find a safe dose.
A setting in which two neighbouring subduction zones operate side by side, with two plates sinking into the mantle and interacting.
The fruit fly genus, especially Drosophila melanogaster, a small insect widely used in genetics and biology because it breeds fast and is easy to modify genetically.
A technique that applies a sequence of control pulses to a qubit to cancel out noise from its surroundings and extend its coherence.
An unhealthy imbalance in the community of microbes living in the body, such as the gut, compared with a normal state.
A large protein that links the inner skeleton of muscle cells to their surrounding membrane, protecting fibres during contraction. Its loss causes Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
An enzyme that attaches ubiquitin tags to specific target proteins, often marking them for destruction. Hundreds of different types decide which proteins are tagged.
The jumping of electrons from one atomic site to a neighbouring one in a solid; the pattern of hops shapes the material's energy bands.
A series of protein complexes in the inner mitochondrial membrane that pass electrons along and pump protons, creating the energy store used to make ATP.
When an excited electron in a semiconductor falls back and fills an empty state, called a hole, losing its energy as light or heat. Slow loss helps solar cells.
A small unit of energy: the energy one electron gains when moved across a voltage of one volt. Widely used for bond, band and particle energies.
The process by which a cell takes in material from outside by folding its membrane inward to form a small bubble inside the cell.
An organism whose cells have a nucleus and other internal membrane-bound compartments, including animals, plants, fungi and many single-celled forms.
The time after treatment during which a patient has no defined bad event, such as cancer growth, return or death.
A T cell that has lost much of its killing and multiplying ability after long exposure to antigen, as in chronic infection or cancer.
A DNA variant linked to how much a gene is expressed. Used to connect disease-linked variants to the genes they likely affect.
A form of regulated cell death driven by iron and the damaging oxidation of fats in cell membranes. It differs from apoptosis.
Statistical analysis that narrows a disease-linked DNA region down to the variants most likely to actually cause the effect.
Describes the first clinical study in which a new drug or treatment is given to people after laboratory and animal testing.
An electron energy band whose energy hardly changes with momentum, so electrons move very slowly and interactions dominate, often producing unusual states.
A grid of light-sensing pixels placed at the focus of a lens, forming the image sensor of a camera, especially an infrared one.
A gene switched on quickly when cells, including nerve cells, are stimulated. Its protein is widely used as a marker of recently active neurons.
A specific group of atoms within a molecule, such as a hydroxyl or amine group, that gives the molecule its characteristic chemical reactions.
A brain scanning method that tracks changes in blood oxygen to show which brain areas are more active during a task.
Making targeted changes to the DNA of living cells, such as cutting, deleting or rewriting a specific sequence, often with CRISPR-based tools.
The amount of genetic variation within a species or population. Higher diversity helps populations adapt to change and avoid inbreeding problems.
The gradual loss of genetic variation in a population or species, often from shrinking or isolated populations, which can go unnoticed while numbers still look healthy.
A study that scans DNA markers across the whole genome in many people to find variants that are more common in those with a trait or disease.
The use of earth science methods, such as study of sediments and landforms, to understand past human activity and environments.
A computer simulation of how rock in the Earth's interior deforms and flows over geological time, used to test what forces move plates and shape the surface.
A cell in the developing gonad that surrounds and nurtures germ cells; it becomes a Sertoli cell in testes or a granulosa cell in ovaries and directs sex development.
Glutathione peroxidase 4: an enzyme that repairs oxidised fats in cell membranes. It is the main protector against ferroptosis.
A very small neuron. In the cerebellum these are the most numerous neurons in the brain and relay incoming signals to Purkinje cells.
An enzyme released by killer T cells and natural killer cells that enters target cells, usually through perforin pores, and triggers their death.
A single layer of carbon atoms arranged in a honeycomb pattern. It is extremely thin, strong and conducts electricity very well.
The breaking up of a continuous natural habitat into smaller, isolated patches, often by farming, roads or building, which cuts animal movement and gene flow.
The voltage across a conductor, sideways to the current, divided by the current, when a magnetic field is applied. Its quantized values reveal topological states.
A set of gene variants on one chromosome region that are inherited together as a block from one parent.
The part of life spent in good health, free of serious disease or disability, as opposed to total lifespan.
A group of Asgard archaea, microbes thought to be among the closest living relatives of the ancestor of all complex cells.
A molecule made of linked rings that twist into a spiral, giving it a left- or right-handed shape.
A sequencing method that captures which parts of the genome touch each other in 3D space, used to map genome folding.
A diet in which a large share of calories comes from fat, used in animal studies to cause obesity or study how nutrition affects metabolism and inflammation.
An animal's ability to return to its home site, such as a nest, from distant or unfamiliar places.
A mouse given human cells, tissues or genes, often a human immune system, so human disease and treatments can be studied in a living animal.
One of two or more versions of a genetic locus that occupy the same position but have unrelated DNA sequences, unlike ordinary alleles, which are similar versions of one gene.
Rock formed when molten rock (magma or lava) cools and solidifies. Slow cooling deep underground gives larger crystals.
A drug that blocks brake molecules on immune cells, such as PD-1, letting T cells attack cancer more strongly.
Performed by computer simulation or analysis rather than in living things or test tubes.
Supplied by a separate molecule rather than being part of the same molecule. For example, a template provided on a different RNA from the enzyme.
A plant or animal strain made genetically almost uniform through many generations of self-crossing or breeding between close relatives.
An electron jump between energy levels in a crystal that also needs a lattice vibration to supply momentum. Such jumps absorb and emit light weakly.
A technique that fires neutrons at a sample and measures the energy and momentum they gain or lose, mapping vibrations and magnetic excitations such as magnons.
Chronic, low-grade inflammation that develops with age without obvious infection, thought to contribute to many age-related diseases.
A protein complex inside immune cells that senses danger and activates inflammatory signals such as IL-1 beta, sometimes leading to cell death.
A quantum jump of electrons from one energy band to another driven by a strong electric field, such as an intense laser pulse.
Immune-related adverse event: inflammation of normal organs, such as gut, skin, liver or glands, caused by immune checkpoint drugs.
Immune-related colitis: inflammation of the colon caused by immune checkpoint drugs, one of the most common serious side effects of these treatments.
Isoursodeoxycholic acid: a form of the bile acid ursodeoxycholic acid that is produced by gut bacteria.
Shaping stone, such as flint, by striking off flakes to make tools. Knappable stone breaks in a controlled way suitable for this.
An organism or cell in which a specific gene has been deliberately inactivated, so researchers can see what that gene does.
A material with a regular array of localized magnetic moments that interact with mobile electrons, which can produce heavy electrons and unusual quantum phases.
N-lactoyl-phenylalanine: a molecule formed from lactate and the amino acid phenylalanine. It rises after intense exercise and can reduce food intake.
A form of the enzyme that converts lactate and pyruvate into each other, common in heart muscle where it favours turning lactate into pyruvate.
Copying of the DNA strand that runs the opposite way to the moving replication fork. It is made backwards in short pieces that are later joined.
An immune cell resident in the epidermis that samples substances and microbes in the skin and helps control local immune responses.
A semiconductor compound of lead and sulfur that absorbs infrared light, used in infrared detectors often as tiny crystals.
The lowest-risk category on the IUCN Red List, given to species judged widespread and abundant enough not to be at risk of extinction.
A tiny fat-based particle used to carry RNA or other cargo into cells, as in mRNA vaccines.
Damaging oxidation of fats, especially in cell membranes, by reactive molecules. Uncontrolled, it drives ferroptosis.
An electron state confined to a small region rather than spread through the whole material, so it does not carry current.
A specific place in the genome, such as the position of a gene or a DNA region linked to a trait.
Lipopolysaccharide: a molecule from the outer wall of many bacteria that strongly triggers inflammation. Often used to mimic infection in experiments.
Computer methods that learn patterns from data to make predictions or decisions, rather than following rules written by hand.
A quantum of a spin wave: a collective ripple in the orientation of electron spins travelling through a magnetic material, carrying energy and spin.
The thick layer of hot, mostly solid rock between a planet's crust and core. It slowly flows and is the source of most magmas.
A small seabird of the North Atlantic that travels long distances over the ocean and returns reliably to its burrow, making it a model for studying navigation.
A rock that was blasted off Mars by an impact and later fell to Earth. These are the only Martian samples available on Earth.
A method that measures the mass of molecules very precisely, used to identify and quantify proteins, peptides and other compounds.
A sensor protein inside cells, related to RIG-I, that recognises long double-stranded viral RNA and starts an interferon-based antiviral response.
A genus of legume plants including alfalfa. Medicago truncatula is a standard model for studying root nodules and nitrogen fixation.
A region of actively dividing, undifferentiated plant cells that produces new tissues, such as at root and shoot tips.
A temporary embryonic kidney that forms before the permanent kidney. It largely regresses, but its tissues contribute to the male reproductive ducts and possibly to the gonads.
Large-scale measurement of the small molecules (metabolites) in a cell, tissue or body fluid, giving a snapshot of chemical activity.
Any multicellular animal. The term is used to contrast animals with single-celled organisms such as yeast or bacteria.
Addition of a small chemical tag (a methyl group), especially to DNA, which can affect whether nearby genes are switched on.
An early product in the pathway that makes cholesterol and related molecules. Statins block its production.
Cell-surface molecules found on nearly all cells that display short protein fragments from inside the cell to killer T cells.
The whole community of microbes, such as bacteria, viruses and fungi, living in a particular place like the gut, and their genes.
The resident immune cells of the brain and spinal cord. They clear debris, prune connections between nerve cells and react to injury and disease.
The process by which proteins made in the cytoplasm are moved into mitochondria through dedicated membrane channels. Most mitochondrial proteins are encoded in the nucleus and need this route.
A protein in the inner membrane of mitochondria that imports pyruvate, the product of sugar breakdown, so it can be burned for energy.
The larger-scale interference pattern made when two similar lattices are overlaid with a slight twist or mismatch. In layered crystals it creates a new superlattice that reshapes electron behaviour.
An imaging method that maps the energies and directions of electrons knocked out of a material by light, revealing how electrons move inside it.
A membrane transport protein that carries lactate, pyruvate and similar small molecules into or out of cells.
A material that should conduct according to simple band theory but insulates because strong repulsion between electrons stops them from moving onto already occupied sites.
The main receptor through which morphine and similar drugs relieve pain. It also mediates their side effects, such as breathing depression and dependence.
Combining several large-scale molecular measurements, such as genes, RNA, proteins and metabolites, from the same samples to get a fuller picture.
A relationship between two species in which both benefit.

A family of two-dimensional materials made of thin layers of transition metal carbides or nitrides, usually made by etching out a layer from a parent crystal. Studied for batteries, electronics and shielding.
A channel or pore only a few nanometres wide, through which ions or molecules pass. Such channels are used in filtration and separation membranes.
A strip of material only a few nanometres wide, such as a narrow strip of graphene, whose electronic properties depend on its width and edges.
A serious bowel disease mainly of premature newborns in which parts of the gut wall become inflamed and die.
A pattern of colour or markings on a flower, often visible only in ultraviolet light, that leads visiting insects or birds towards the nectar.
A plant gland, usually in the flower, that produces and releases nectar to attract and reward pollinating animals.
A new protein fragment, not normally made by the body, that the immune system can see as foreign. Often arises from mutations in cancer.
Conversion of nitrogen gas from the air into ammonia, a form living things can use. Some bacteria do this, often in partnership with plants.
A sensor protein that forms the best-known inflammasome, responding to many danger signals and linked to gout, atherosclerosis and age-related inflammation.
A small growth on the roots of legumes where nitrogen-fixing bacteria live and work in partnership with the plant.
A type of jumping genetic element, such as LINE-1, that lacks long repeated ends and inserts its copy by reverse transcribing its RNA directly at the target DNA site.
A transcription factor that switches on many antioxidant and detoxifying genes when cells face oxidative stress.
An insect of the order Odonata, the dragonflies and damselflies. Their larvae live in water, making them useful indicators of freshwater health.
A short piece of DNA made on the lagging strand during replication. Many such pieces are later joined into one continuous strand.
Building molecules directly on a clean metal surface, often under vacuum, to make structures too large or reactive to make in solution.
A method that makes chosen nerve cells sensitive to light by giving them light-gated proteins, so researchers can switch them on or off with light.
The region around an atom or molecule where an electron is likely to be found, with a set energy. How these regions overlap and mix decides how atoms bond.
An organic compound containing a carbon-chlorine bond. Many are cheap and stable but hard to activate for chemical reactions.
The main way mitochondria make the cell's energy currency, ATP, using oxygen and a chain of membrane proteins.
A form of oxygen atom with a different number of neutrons, such as oxygen-16 or oxygen-18. Their ratios act as fingerprints of a sample's origin, temperature or water history.
A voltage-gated calcium channel at many nerve endings. Calcium entry through it triggers release of chemical messengers.
A lake that existed in the past but has since dried up, often leaving sediments that record former wetter climates.
The upper part of the vertebrate forebrain. In mammals it forms the cerebral cortex; in birds it is organised differently but supports comparable complex cognition.
A symmetry in which a system behaves the same when added electrons are swapped for missing electrons (holes). When broken, electron- and hole-rich states behave differently.
No remaining invasive cancer found in tissue removed at surgery after treatment given beforehand.
A model in which tumour tissue from a patient is grown in an immunodeficient mouse, keeping much of the original tumour's features.
A brake receptor on T cells that weakens their activity when bound by its partner molecules. Drugs blocking it are used in cancer immunotherapy.
A long-predicted form of carbon sheet made of five- and seven-membered rings instead of graphene's six-membered rings.
A choice based on interpreting sensory information, such as judging whether a stimulus is present or which category it belongs to.
A protein released by killer T cells and natural killer cells that punches pores in the membrane of target cells.
The study of rocks: their minerals, textures, origin and history.
Phenome-wide association study: testing a genetic variant against many traits and diseases at once to find all the outcomes it is linked to.
A highly toxic gas used in industry to make plastics and chemicals. Safer liquid or solid chemicals are often used in its place.
The science and technology of generating, guiding and detecting light, as in lasers, optical fibres and light-based chips.
A drug-like molecule that changes shape when light of a certain colour hits it, so its activity can be switched on or off with light.
An enzyme activated by double-stranded RNA during viral infection. It shuts down protein production in the cell, which helps block virus replication.
A clinical trial that tests several treatments under one shared plan, allowing arms to be added or dropped over time.
A widely used, chlorine-containing plastic found in pipes, cables and medical tubing.
The retention by adult cells of gene activity that reflects where in the body they came from, helping guide regeneration to restore the right structures.
A baby's age counted from the first day of the mother's last menstrual period, so it equals gestational age plus time since birth. Used to track preterm infants.
Publicly recording a study's hypotheses and analysis plan before seeing the data, to reduce selective reporting and false findings.
A lipid signalling molecule made from arachidonic acid by cyclooxygenase enzymes. It regulates inflammation, fever, pain and the growth of many cell types.
A visible clump of misfolded or aggregated protein inside a cell, often seen in brain cells in neurodegenerative diseases.
Large-scale study of the proteins in a cell or tissue, usually measured by mass spectrometry, including their amounts and modifications.
The balance of making, folding, maintaining and breaking down proteins in a cell, which keeps the protein supply healthy.
A large neuron with a highly branched, fan-shaped dendrite tree in the cerebellar cortex. It provides the only output of the cerebellar cortex and is key for motor coordination.
An immune sensor protein that forms an inflammasome when certain cell signalling pathways are disturbed. Mutations in its gene cause familial Mediterranean fever.
An inflammatory form of programmed cell death, triggered by inflammasomes, in which the cell bursts and releases inflammatory signals.
The ability of a quantum system to keep a well-defined combination of states over time. Losing it destroys stored quantum information.
A network that links quantum devices with light so they can share quantum information, for secure communication or distributed quantum computing.
The basic unit of quantum information. Unlike a normal bit, it can be in a mix of 0 and 1 at the same time.
A molecule or atom with an unpaired electron, making it highly reactive. Radical reactions are used to build bonds and make plastics.
Any of the 17 metallic elements made up of scandium, yttrium and the lanthanides. They have unusual magnetic and optical properties and are used in magnets and electronics.
A DNA difference carried by only a small share of people, usually under about one percent. Single ones can have larger effects but are hard to study statistically.
An electronic chip under an image sensor that collects and processes the signal from each pixel.
A change in RNA, such as by editing, that alters which amino acid is coded, so the resulting protein differs from the DNA's instructions.
The International Union for Conservation of Nature's global inventory of threatened species, the main list that ranks species by extinction risk, from Least Concern to Extinct.
The large group of proteins that work together at the replication fork to unwind DNA and copy both strands.
A spectroscopy that tunes X-rays to an energy that a chosen atom absorbs strongly and measures the energy they lose on scattering, revealing electronic and magnetic excitations such as magnons.
A DNA segment that copies itself through an RNA step and inserts the new copy elsewhere in the genome. Such elements make up much of many genomes.
Soil bacteria that live in root nodules of legumes such as beans and turn nitrogen gas into forms the plant can use.
A zone where the Earth's crust is being pulled apart, forming a long valley that may eventually split a continent and open a new ocean.
A sensor protein inside cells that detects viral RNA and triggers an antiviral response, including production of type I interferons.
Changing specific letters in an RNA after it is made from DNA, so the protein produced can differ from what the gene encodes.
Reactive oxygen species: highly reactive oxygen-containing molecules made during normal metabolism and stress. They signal at low levels and cause damage at high levels.
The region of a plant genome that controls self-incompatibility. It carries matching pollen and pistil genes whose many variants decide which pollen is rejected.
The major fault in California where the Pacific and North American plates slide past each other horizontally, causing frequent earthquakes.
Imaging methods that move a very sharp tip over a surface to map it, down to single atoms and their electronic states.
A technique that scans a sharp metal tip just above a conducting surface and measures the tiny quantum tunnelling current, imaging individual atoms and electronic states.
A genetic system in many flowering plants that stops pollen from fertilising the same plant or close relatives, promoting outbreeding.
A flexible, heat-stable polymer with a backbone of alternating silicon and oxygen atoms, used in oils, rubbers, sealants and medical implants.
A highly reactive, positively charged silicon species that strongly grabs electron-rich atoms such as oxygen and chlorine.
Methods that measure two or more kinds of molecular data, such as RNA and open chromatin, from the same individual cell, linking gene control to gene activity.
A method that reads which genes are active in thousands of individual cells, so cell types and states can be told apart.
Microscopy methods that track individual molecules one at a time, often with fluorescent labels, to see how they move and interact.
A device in which one molecule bridges two electrodes, so electric current through that single molecule can be measured.
A common difference at a single DNA letter between people. Such markers are used to map genes linked to traits and diseases.
The share of differences in a trait between people that can be explained by common DNA markers measured together across the genome.
A flaw in a crystal, such as a missing atom next to a foreign atom, that can trap electrons and act as a qubit.
A set of methods that measure which genes are active in tissue while keeping track of where each cell or spot sits in the section.
A standard measure of a light detector's sensitivity that adjusts for its size and bandwidth, measured in units called Jones. Higher means fainter signals can be seen.
A flow of electron spin, the tiny magnetic property of electrons, which may occur with or without a flow of electric charge.
A device of magnetic layers whose electrical resistance depends on how their magnetizations line up, used to detect and inject spin currents.
A system that links a quantum spin, which stores information, with particles of light, which carry it, so quantum information can be transferred.
Electronics that use electron spin, not just charge, to store and process information, as in computer hard-disk read heads and magnetic memory.
A transcription factor that senses cholesterol levels and switches on genes for making and taking up cholesterol when levels are low.
A spatial transcriptomics method that captures RNA on a chip of DNA-barcoded spots, mapping gene activity across a tissue section at very fine resolution.
A family of cells, sharing a developmental origin, that become able to make steroid hormones such as testosterone, oestrogen or cortisol, as in the gonads and adrenal glands.
A deep brain region in the basal ganglia involved in movement control, habits and reward. It is the area most damaged in Huntington's disease.
A large change in DNA structure, usually at least 50 base pairs, such as a deletion, duplication, insertion or inversion.
The process at converging plate boundaries in which one tectonic plate sinks beneath another into the mantle, creating deep trenches, volcanoes and large earthquakes.
An animal's use of the Sun's position, corrected for time of day by its internal clock, to hold a travel direction.
An organism living in close, long-term association with another organism of a different species, often inside its cells or tissues.
A membrane protein of the SNARE family that helps vesicles fuse with the cell membrane, which is needed for release of nerve messengers.
A partnership in which two microbes depend on each other to feed, often because one uses the waste products of the other.
The surface receptor that lets a T cell recognize a specific protein fragment displayed by MHC molecules.
A short DNA sequence repeated many times in a row. The number of repeats often differs between people and can change how nearby genes work.
A small sulfur-containing molecule found in high amounts in many tissues and in the diet. It has roles in bile, cell volume and protection against stress.
The front-most part of the vertebrate brain, which forms the cerebral hemispheres in mammals and their counterparts in birds and fish.
A type of helper T cell that makes the signal protein IL-17. It helps fight some bacteria and fungi but also drives many inflammatory and autoimmune diseases, such as psoriasis.
A memory T cell that stays in one tissue, such as skin or gut, instead of circulating in blood. It reacts fast to a repeat threat but can also keep local inflammation going.
The exit side of the Golgi apparatus, where newly made proteins and fats are sorted into packages and sent to their destinations.
A small RNA molecule that carries a specific amino acid to the ribosome and matches it to the code in messenger RNA during protein synthesis.
A cell-surface protein that binds transferrin, the blood protein that carries iron, and brings it into the cell.
The release of chemical messengers from a nerve ending when vesicles fuse with its membrane, passing a signal to the next cell.
Regulatory T cell: a T cell that dampens immune responses and prevents attacks on the body's own tissues. Usually marked by the protein FOXP3.
A small protein attached to other proteins as a tag that can mark them for breakdown or change their activity or location.
Attachment of ubiquitin tags to a protein, which can mark it for breakdown or change its function. Also called ubiquitination.
A large British research resource of about half a million volunteers with genetic data, health records, scans and samples, open to researchers.
A surface-science method that fires short pulses of molecules at a surface and times when they leave, measuring their speed, to work out reaction rates and binding energies.
The ability to learn new sounds by hearing and copying others, as in human speech and songbird song. Most animals have only inborn calls.
An exercise model in which rodents can run on a wheel in their cage as much as they choose, rather than being forced.
Reliable access to enough safe water for people, farming, industry and nature, which depends on infrastructure, management and demand, not only on rainfall.
Reading the complete DNA sequence of an organism's genome, including the non-coding regions between genes.
A solid-like arrangement in which electrons, kept apart by their mutual repulsion, settle into a regular lattice. It forms when repulsion outweighs their kinetic energy at low density.
A cell communication system that controls growth, development and stem cell maintenance. Abnormal activity is common in cancer.
A genus of African clawed frogs. Their large eggs and egg extracts are widely used to study development, cell division and DNA replication.
A transcription co-activator controlled by the Hippo pathway and by cell crowding and stiffness. It helps cells sense their surroundings and decide whether to grow.
A unit of length equal to one ten-billionth of a metre, about the size of an atom. Used for atomic distances and crystal spacings.
